title: OSHA Basics & Incident / Near-Miss Reporting

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Shop bulletin board: OSHA poster, emergency numbers, SDS binder hanging beside it. Danny standing next to it, medium shot.
scenes.says: I'm Danny. Before we talk rules, know where three things live: the OSHA poster, the Safety Data Sheet binder, and the emergency numbers. They're right here. Knowing the rules is what keeps your work safe and planned, and knowing how to report is how we keep the next person from getting hurt.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Close-up on Danny at the bulletin board.
scenes.says: OSHA is the federal agency that sets and enforces workplace safety rules. Some states run their own plans that can be stricter. Two sets of rules apply to us. 1910, general industry, covers maintenance in existing buildings, like relamping and lockout. 1926 covers construction, and many retrofits count as construction. Your supervisor will tell you which applies. When in doubt, follow the stricter one.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Danny at the bulletin board, pointing to a printed NFPA 70E cover graphic.
scenes.on_screen: NFPA 70E = how to meet electrical safety rules
scenes.says: You'll also hear about NFPA 70E, the Standard for Electrical Safety in the Workplace. Here's the simple way to think about it. OSHA says what has to be achieved. 70E gives the detailed methods for how to do it.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Danny opening the SDS binder to a product page; cut-in of a cleaner can label.
scenes.on_screen: Your rights: training, PPE, SDS, report without retaliation
scenes.says: You have rights. A workplace free of recognized serious hazards. Training you understand. Required PPE. Access to the Safety Data Sheets for chemicals you use. And the right to report injuries and hazards without retaliation. Your part: follow the rules, wear and care for your PPE, report promptly, and never bypass a safety device or use damaged gear.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Reenactment in an office corridor: a tech on a stepladder lets a lens slip; it drops into the coned-off area below. Nobody hurt. Danny voice-over.
scenes.on_screen: Near miss = could have caused harm, but didn't
scenes.says: Here's a near miss. The lens slipped and fell into the barricaded area. Nobody got hurt. That's because of the barricade, not luck. Near misses are free lessons. For every serious injury there are usually many near misses that came first. Report them, and we fix the cause before someone gets hurt.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Same corridor. The crew steps aside; Danny with them. Over-the-shoulder shot of a phone showing the company near-miss form.
scenes.on_screen: 1. People first  2. Make it safe  3. Call supervisor  4. Report in writing same day  5. Preserve the scene  6. Cooperate
scenes.says: Here's how we report. Take care of people first, and call 911 for anything serious. Make the scene safe. Call your supervisor right away, by phone, not just text, for any injury, any shock, or real damage. Write it up the same day on the company form or app. Keep the damaged tool or lamp and take photos if it's safe. Then help the investigation. It's about causes, not blame.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Tight shot of the phone screen as the tech types; Danny voice-over.
scenes.on_screen:
Weak: "Ladder was bad, almost fell."
Strong: date, time, place, people, equipment and asset #, what happened, what you did
scenes.says: Write facts, not opinions. Ladder was bad, almost fell, tells us nothing. A good report says the date and time, the exact room, who was there, the equipment and its asset number, what you were doing, what happened, and what you did right after. Like: right rear foot slipped on a wet floor that had no sign, ladder tagged out, no injury.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Back at the bulletin board, close-up on Danny.
scenes.says: One safety rule I want you to remember. Anyone who gets an electrical shock gets checked by a medical professional, even if they feel fine. Current can cause internal injuries and heart rhythm problems that don't show up right away. And the company has to report serious injuries to OSHA within hours, so your supervisor needs to hear about them immediately.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.on_screen: Now read the lesson and take the quiz
scenes.says: Report every injury, shock, damage and near miss the same day. Make it specific. Now read the lesson and take the quiz.

production_notes: Bulletin board needs a current OSHA poster, a generic emergency-numbers sheet (no real phone numbers legible), and an SDS binder. Near-miss reenactment: lens drops into a coned/taped area with nobody beneath it; use a plastic prop lens. Phone screen shows a generic near-miss form, no company branding beyond a placeholder. Lesson numbers referenced: fatalities reported to OSHA within 8 hours; hospitalization, amputation or eye loss within 24 hours (29 CFR 1904.39) - can be added as an on-screen callout in scene 8 if wanted.
